articleTitle: Definition and measurement of voltage flicker (in lighting)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Power Systems Measurement
abstract: The level of annoyance suffered by consumers due to lighting flicker is dependent on the amplitude, shape and repetition frequency of the voltage changes which cause it. The quantification of such disturbances in terms of consumer annoyance proved difficult in the past due to the lack of an agreed definition. This has recently been overcome by the acceptance by the IEC of a definition of flicker severity. This defines the threshold of flicker perceptibility for 50% of the population in terms of percentage amplitude modulation on a 50 Hz carrier using a 60 Watt 240 volt tungsten filament coiled-lamp.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Power Systems Measurement
abstract: The selection and reduction of available data is a necessary feature of any measurement system in order to avoid presenting the end user with an excessive volume of data from which the required information is then to be extracted. The way in which the available data is then interpreted will be determined by the nature of that data together with the purpose for which the measurement was made. In the case of power system harmonic measurements both these factors are of importance, particularly in relation to the operation of currently available microprocessor based harmonic analysers. These use analytic techniques to generate large volumes of data with associated problems of interpretation and of comparison with results obtained from a previous generation of sequential, analogue instruments.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Converting data into information (power system harmonic analysis)
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Power Systems Measurement
abstract: Digital instrumentation for the measurement of power systems signals have been available for many years. Some instruments are based on existing equipment which have been modified to deal with power frequencies, while others have been devised specially. The authors show that one area where these instruments are used is in the harmonic analysis of power system signals.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Remote location of faulted 11 kV cable sections
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Power Systems Measurement
abstract: In order to restored supplies to customers following faults on 11 kV distribution networks, the faulted section of cable has to be identified and manual switching performed. The switching is to separate the faulted section from the healthy sections of the feeder and to reconnect supply to the healthy sections. This process results in an average supply interruption time of 1/sup 1///sub 2/ hours per fault, one third of which is the time required to locate the faulted section. The remote faulted section location system outlined by the author is an improvement on previous methods and operates by detecting the passage of earth fault current at the distribution substations and then sending the information to the primary substation using the faulted 11 kV cable as the communication channel.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Graphic recordings of power disturbances: some recent developments and interpretations
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronics in Power Systems Measurement
abstract: Electronic devices can be damaged or disrupted by deviations from the expected AC mains voltage waveform and frequency. These deviations can include increases and decreases in RMS voltage (commonly referred to as surges and sags, respectively), high-frequency high-amplitude events (commonly referred to as impulses), changes in the voltage waveshape, harmonic distortion in the waveshape, and superimposed low-amplitude noise. The author examines recent developments in the field of simultaneous oscillographic recordings of power disturbances. He argues that as more practical experience accumulates with graphic recordings of mains disturbances, additional models and signatures may be developed which will further assist in disturbance diagnosis and mitigation.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
